<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I've read it. Sections 1 to 5 are strong corrections and should change how the Halden pilot is read. Sections 6 to 8 then reach a conclusion that the comment's own numbers, and the Varden trial it cites, don't support.

## What the comment claims

Using the Halden microdata, the authors make five corrections:

- **Attrition.** Seven of the nine withdrawals came after the reduced schedule began, not during preparation. Six of the nine cited workload or output as the reason.
- **Output measure.** In the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index in 19 cases, by 3.8 points on average.
- **Hours.** In the 27 organisations with time tracking, actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%.
- **Combined.** Record-based output divided by actual hours, available for 17 organisations, gives a per-hour gain of +10.8% instead of +23.4%.
- **Revenue and sector.** Real revenue fell about 2.6%. The claim of gains in every sector is an artifact of the per-hour metric.

They then argue three further points:

- The remaining gain is a novelty effect, inferred from the decay in reported energy.
- The Varden meetings analysis should not be cited as a mechanism.
- Per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

## Arithmetic

Most figures check out:

- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 → +10.8%; 34.8/40.4 → −13.9%; 34.6/40.3 → −14.1%. All correct.
- **Revenue:** 1.014/1.041 → −2.6% real. Correct.

Two figures don't reconcile.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Four scheduled 8-hour days, plus 0.7 extra hours a day, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, comes to about 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. Starting from the baseline daily average of about 8.06 gives about 36.6. The 34.6 total implies only about 0.25 extra hours a day. Possible explanations include averaging over different denominators, part-time staff, or staggered schedules, but the authors need to explain it. If 36.4 is right, actual hours fell only about 10% and the corrected per-hour gain shrinks further. If 34.6 is right, the decomposition is wrong.

**The novelty extrapolation gives the wrong month.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6. A linear decline at that rate reaches zero around month 8.7, not month 10. This is minor next to the larger problem: a straight line through two points is a weak basis for any forecast.

## What holds, and how much it weighs

**Attrition is the most important finding.** It corrects a factual statement in the Halden paper, using Halden's own data. A per-protocol sample that excludes organisations withdrawing for output reasons after treatment began is biased in a known direction.

What is missing is a bounding analysis. For example: assign the nine withdrawals an output index of 85, 90 and 95, and report the 70-organisation estimate under each. Without that, the size of the attrition bias is not quantified. Note also that **the abstract says the first three problems are corrected, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours.** The 10.8% figure is still computed on survivors, as Section 6 itself concedes.

**The manager bias is well supported.** Nineteen of 23 organisations went the same way, which is unlikely by chance (sign test p ≈ 0.003). Because it is a within-organisation comparison, it survives the concern that organisations submitting records differ from those that didn't.

One caveat runs the other way. Some of the "records" are billable hours delivered. That measures hours worked, not output, so it falls mechanically when hours fall and biases record-based output downward for professional-services firms. The authors should show the comparison with hours-based records excluded.

**The hours correction is solid, subject to the decomposition query above.**

**The revenue point is correct.** CPI is a rough deflator for a mix of businesses and non-profits, but the direction and approximate size are right.

**The sector point is correct in substance.** The retail figure from records rests on only three organisations, so it supports the conclusion but can't carry much weight alone.

## Where it overreaches

**1. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the comment's own figures and by the trial it cites.**

After two of its corrections, the comment's own best estimate is still a +10.8% gain. It then attributes that residual to novelty without testing the attribution. The Varden trial addresses all three proposed artifacts at once:

- it was randomised, so there was no self-selection or survivor sample;
- output came from administrative records, not managers;
- hours came from timesheets.

It found +12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing offices (CI +6.9 to +18.4), over nine months, which is longer than Halden ran.

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". It doesn't mention the case-processing result, which comes from the same trial with the same design. Using one arm of a trial and leaving out the other because of which way it points is the kind of selection the comment criticises in Halden.

**2. Novelty is an open question, not a settled one.**

The energy decline is a fair reason for concern; I raised it about Halden myself. But the argument has two gaps:

- Energy is not productivity. The comment assumes the two move together without showing it.
- Varden's control staff also knew a trial was running. That weakens a pure "being observed" explanation, though it doesn't rule out novelty from the change itself.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is fair as a reason to report durability as unknown. It doesn't license concluding the effect is zero. The honest position is that persistence beyond six to nine months is unknown, and Varden's 24-month follow-up will settle much of it.

**3. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis.**

The Varden authors did not cite meetings as a mechanism. They said it was unregistered, rested on seven offices, "cannot establish a mechanism", and that they had registered a confirmatory test.

The seven offices were also not "selected after the results were known". They are the whole treated case-processing stratum. What was decided late was collecting the meetings data, not choosing which offices to include.

Varden has already handled this as an open hypothesis with a confirmatory test registered. Dismissing it before that test reports is closing the question too early.

## Where the evidence stands across the three papers

**Settled enough to report as findings:**

- **Halden's 23.4% overstates the effect.** Survivor bias, manager rounding and the scheduled-hours denominator all push it up, and Halden's statement about when organisations withdrew was wrong.
- **Coverage-bound work loses output.** Where output depends on staff being present, cutting hours reduces output per employee by about a tenth and worsens service. Both studies point the same way, and Varden's estimate is randomised.
- **Hours-based per-hour gains look better than they are.** In coverage-bound work they are probably partly a utilisation effect: busier staff, longer queues.
- **Non-coverage work shows a real per-hour gain in the short run.** In work not tied to presence, output per actual hour rose by roughly 10 to 13% over six to nine months. Two independent routes land in the same place: the Varden RCT (12.5%) and the corrected Halden subset (10.8%). Taking the hours query and any unrecorded hours into account, the true figure may be somewhat lower.

**Still open:**

- Whether the per-hour gain lasts beyond nine months.
- How much of it comes from rest and how much from cutting low-value time such as meetings.
- What Halden's attrition does to the overall estimate once the withdrawals are bounded.
- Whether any of this generalises beyond these two populations.

The comment's recommendations for future evaluations are sound and I'd endorse them unchanged: record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, at least 18 months of follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis of all enrolled organisations.

I can draft a reply to the comment, a referee report on it, or a one-page evidence summary across the three papers set out as found versus open.
